t: A Little-Known Teaching Strategy That Makes Learning Easier -learning-easier/
q: When you tell students that something is hard, when you label it as hard, then it becomes hard. It becomes exactly what you say it is.
Sadly, students who are behind academically are the most affected. The second they hear you say that something is difficult, they check out.
Just as calling something difficult makes it difficult, calling something doable makes it doable. In other words, if you pretend it’s easy, then it becomes easy.
Now, it's important to point out that the strategy only works if your instruction is up to snuff.
One of the secrets to great teaching, and galloping progress, is to guide your students from one success to the next, all day every day.

t: Why Strict, Fair, Compassionate Accountability Makes You Popular With Students y-makes-you-popular-with-students/
q: You see, when you consistently hold students accountable according to rules and expectations you lay out ahead of time, it makes you the most popular teacher at school.
So when students meet someone that actually does what they say they’re going to do, they can’t help but be affected.

Once you prove to your students that the agreed-upon consequences are the only consequences, and that you’re not going to lecture, scold, glare, admonish, or otherwise take their misbehavior personally, it frees them to truly enjoy your class.
This, in turn, safeguards your relationship with them. In fact, it makes their trust and belief in you, as well as your likability, even stronger.
You must enforce your consequences like a referee rather than a judge.
So that your students will not only never hold your faithful accountability against you. They’ll love you for it.
x: Consistent, promised accountability tends to make teachers not just respected but genuinely popular with students.
Students respect rare integrity—teachers who reliably follow through on what they say they'll do.
Students feel liberated once they know consequences are the only consequences and enforcement is never personal.
Linsin describes the surprise many teachers feel when consistent accountability makes them among the most popular teachers at school, not merely respected but genuinely well-liked.
Enforcement must be delivered like a neutral referee, without lecturing, scolding, or added personal commentary, for the effect to hold.

q: So: arguments make for rich school cultures — not just arguments in our classrooms, but arguments in our meetings. But what does this actually look like? Thankfully, there's a school in Wisconsin that's laid out a pretty good example of this.

Now, notice: by asking for the most impactful strategies, Sankey set things up to get argumentative. (Good, clear prompts are critical in setting up good argumentative conversations.) It's also important to note that this question was directly linked with the school improvement plan at Patty's school. (Typically, SIPs can be lifeless, gargantuan things, so approaching them argumentatively is a smart move for getting a staff intellectually engaged.
(The articles help ensure that folks will make evidence-based arguments rather than relying on opinion.)

This is where the arguing happened. Even though Patty called these table conversations “Academic Collaborative Conversations” when she was leading the PD — and that was probably a smart move, as the word “argument” is so wrought with baggage that simply hearing it is bound to turn some PD participants off at first — make no mistake about it: these teachers were arguing. These conversations were rational, evidence-based, “let's get to the bottom of this” affairs — they were earnestly and amicably argumentative.

This final application piece is a smart way to move from the big, pressing question into a manageable, “can't miss” application. When teachers are as busy as we are, such applications are inseparable from PD that actually creates change.

t: 5 Signs You've Lost Control Of Your Class (But Don't Know It)
q: It’s the scores of teachers who have lost control of their class but continue to plow forward.
Well, after coaching hundreds of teachers over the past couple of years, and asking this very question, I now know the answer: It’s because they don’t realize they’ve lost control.

If you feel you have no choice but to give instruction while your students are talking (because of the time and trouble it takes to get them quiet), then you have very little influence over their behavior.
If you find yourself repeating much of what you say, and reminding your students again and again about the same things, then you’ve effectively trained them to tune you out.
In well-run, well-behaved classrooms, the teacher focuses on delivering great lessons while the burden of listening and learning falls in toto onto the shoulders of students.
The notion that stress and frustration are just part of the job is a lie.
x: Many teachers who have lost control of their class don't recognize it because chronic disorder has become normalized to them.
After coaching hundreds of teachers, Linsin identifies a recurring pattern.
Talking over students while giving instruction is identified as clear evidence of lost teacher influence.
Constant reminding and repeating trains students to tune the teacher out entirely.
Working harder than the students signals an imbalance where the burden of learning has shifted away from them.

t: How to Improve School Cultures, Part 3: Better Meetings
q: If we want to improve the cultures of our schools, we'd be smart to look not just at the way we lead, but also the way we meet. Whether meeting one-on-one or as a whole district, informally or formally, as a PLC or as a grade-level team, meetings create culture.

First, it's tricky for school meetings, especially at the whole-staff level, to meet all of these requirements. In plenty of schools, meetings are dictated by contract-defined school calendars. When you only get a single one-hour meeting with the whole staff per month, there's bound to be more than one person responsible, and there's bound to be so much to talk about that you'll cram a month's worth of things into the allotted time frame.
The preceding paragraph is the default for meetings in schools. It's what happens when all of us are doing too much.

This is why, in the best schools, leaders work to do what matters most while minimizing or eliminating time spent on everything else. This is at the root of making meetings the kinds of things that improve school cultures. We need to build cultures that ruthlessly eliminate pointless tasks; for tasks that can't be eliminated, we need to satisfice.

There should probably be a whole meeting at the start of each year where a staff brainstorms pointless things and creates shared understanding for how to strategically minimize time spent on these things. The desired outcome? Give ourselves space to do better, saner work.

Arguments, after all, make meetings worth attending. It may seem counterintuitive in an age where we can't seem to argue amicably in the public square, but that's just because we're not doing argument right.
x: Stuart argues that school culture is built not only by how leaders lead but by how staffs meet.
Contract-defined school calendars make the checklist hard to meet, so cram-everything monthly staff meetings are the predictable default rather than a failure of individual leaders.

The deeper fix is cultural: eliminate pointless tasks outright and satisfice on those that cannot be eliminated, so time is protected for what matters most.
A first-of-year staff meeting to brainstorm pointless work would itself pass Godin's test, because no better way exists to create shared understanding about minimizing it.

Focusing the mind on a single sound, movement, or thought has a unique way of calming excitability, restlessness, tension, and stress. In fact, it’s the basis behind the practice of meditation.
Sit up straight (or stand) and place your hand on your stomach as you expand on the inhale and contract on the exhale.
Have them relive that experience by visualizing it, savoring it, and remembering how it felt.

t: How to Improve School Cultures, Part 2: Collins' Level 5 Leadership
q: Woe to us when we can cite Collins' Good to Great even as we habitually impair school cultures through things like blame-shifting, credit-taking, and self-promotion.

In short, Level 5 leaders are the kind of people who look outside the “window” when things go well — they attribute success to external factors — and look in the “mirror” when things don't go well — they take responsibility for failure.
I find so much to be refreshed by here. I don't need to be larger than life to create a better culture in my classroom or school.

But humility is only half of what Collins and his team observed in the good-to-great companies. He writes, “It's equally about ferocious resolve, an almost stoic determination to do whatever needs to be done to make the company great.
What could school cultures be like with a bunch of humble tigers running around? Answer: awesome.
It doesn't take some epic search to find your next Level 5 PLC leader or principal or superintendent or to find the Level 5 leader in yourself.
So: if you want to improve your school culture (and we all need to because cultures are like gardens that need constant tending), Level 5 leadership offers good food for thought.
x: Part 2 of a series on improving school culture, this post applies Jim Collins' Level 5 leadership from Good to Great to schools.

He compiles Collins' descriptions of Level 5 leaders as humble and ferocious, ambitious for the institution rather than themselves, and quick to look in the mirror for failure and out the window for success.
